papers.title: Prompt specificity and iterative behaviour in text-to-music co-creation: a secondary analysis of interaction logs and a framework for perceived creative control
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can lower barriers to musical creation while also shifting consequential decisions away from the user. This study examines that tension through a secondary analysis of the published PAGURI interaction-log prompt corpus and develops a tentative framework for perceived creative control. The analysable corpus contained 304 text-to-music prompts from 24 participants. Musical specificity was operationalised as explicit instrument and technical-parameter markers; iterative continuity was measured with Jaccard similarity between consecutive prompts and checked against TF-IDF cosine similarity. To avoid pseudoreplication, group comparisons were conducted on participant-level summaries rather than treating 304 prompts as independent cases. Role-derived experience groups differed substantially in mean prompt specificity, H(2) = 10.25, p = 0.006, ε 2 = 0.39, and specificity density, H(2) = 11.52, p = 0.003, ε 2 = 0.45, but not in refinement rate, H(2) = 0.24, p = 0.888. At a descriptive Jaccard threshold of 0.20, 46.8% of consecutive pairs were refinements and 53.2% were restarts; because this classification was threshold-sensitive, continuous similarity remained the primary continuity measure. Prompt specificity did not increase systematically across the session: the mean within-person Spearman correlation was ρ = −0.06, and the distribution of participant-level correlations did not differ significantly from zero, W = 89.0, p = 0.374. These findings distinguish the explicit technical-musical information users encode in prompts from the sequential continuity of their prompting behaviour. The paper integrates task structure, system autonomy, model coverage, prior experience, self-efficacy, and psychological ownership into a testable framework for future music-education research. Given the small participant-level sample and role-derived grouping, the empirical findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

# Drama-3-Japanese

[![Base Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Base%20Model-Drama%203-blue)](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) [![Demo Space](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-HuggingFace%20Space-red)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese-Demo)

**Built with Fish Audio**

**Drama-3-Japanese** is a Japanese fine-tune of [Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3). It focuses on single-speaker text-to-speech with optional reference speech, descriptive captions, and Japanese inline tags for expressive delivery.

## 🌟 Key Features

- **Japanese TTS:** Generate speech from Japanese text, with or without additional conditioning.
- **Caption-based voice design:** Describe voice characteristics, emotion, or speaking style in Japanese.
- **Voice cloning:** Clone a voice using up to three reference clips from the same speaker.
- **Japanese inline tags:** Control emotion and delivery with tags such as `[笑いながら]`, `[驚いて]`, or `[怒りを込めて]`. See [the tag list](TAG_LIST.md) for more examples.
- **Upstream compatibility:** Use the same inference code as Drama 3; replace the model path with this checkpoint.

## 🎧 Audio Samples

### 1. Voice Design — Text + Caption

| Text | Caption | Generated Audio |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 本日はお越しいただき、誠にありがとうございます。どうぞごゆっくりお過ごしください。 | 落ち着いた大人の男性。フォーマルな場で、深く響く声で丁寧かつ歓迎の意を込めて話している。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/sample1_1.wav"></audio> |
| 本日はお越しいただき、誠にありがとうございます。どうぞごゆっくりお過ごしください。 | 若く元気な女性の声。カフェの店員のように、明るくハキハキとした少し高めのトーンで話している。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/sample1_2.wav"></audio> |
| すみません！この近くにコンビニってありますか？ちょっと急いでて、道に迷っちゃったみたいで | 低めの声の男性が、丁寧に道を尋ねている。穏やかで礼儀正しく、余裕のある口調。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/sample2_1.wav"></audio> |
| すみません！この近くにコンビニってありますか？ちょっと急いでて、道に迷っちゃったみたいで | 若い女性が、慌てた様子で早口に話している。焦りと不安が声ににじんでいる。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/sample2_2.wav"></audio> |

### 2. Expressive Generation — Text + Caption + Reference Speech + Tags

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| あははっ[笑い]、それ本当に言ってるの？…[呆れたように]まぁ、君らしいけどね。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/clone_ref2.wav"></audio> | 余裕のある大人の男性。親しい相手に対して、くだけた雰囲気で呆れながらも楽しそうに話している。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/tag_gen1.wav"></audio> |
| ゲホッ、ゲホッ[咳き込みながら]…ごめん、少し休ませて。[弱々しく]今日はもう無理みたい。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/clone_ref1.wav"></audio> | 体調が悪く、非常に苦しそうな若い女性。息も絶え絶えに、申し訳なさそうに弱々しい声で話している。 | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese/resolve/main/samples/tag_gen2.wav"></audio> |

## 🚀 Usage

Follow the original [Fish Speech](https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech) instructions or the [SGLang-Omni Drama 3 cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/fishaudio_drama3.html), using this model in place of `fishaudio/drama-3`.

After installing SGLang-Omni with Drama 3 support:

```bash
sgl-omni serve --model-path Aratako/Drama-3-Japanese --port 8000
```

Generate a single-speaker utterance without a reference or caption:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/speech \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":"こんにちは。今日はいい天気ですね。","response_format":"wav"}' \
  --output output.wav
```

## 🛠️ Training

Drama-3-Japanese was fine-tuned from Fish Audio Drama 3 using LoRA on approximately 70,000 hours of Japanese speech data for one epoch. The token embeddings and audio decoder were also trained.

| Hyperparameter | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| LoRA rank / alpha | 32 / 32 |
| Optimizer | AdamW |
| Learning rate (LoRA / embeddings / audio decoder) | 2e-4 / 2e-5 / 5e-5 |

## 📊 Benchmarks

Both models were evaluated with SGLang-Omni at commit [`b658fa671d6a8a01d9b973754300837dff49d22d`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/tree/b658fa671d6a8a01d9b973754300837dff49d22d), using temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9, top-k 30, and a maximum of 2,048 acoustic frames (approximately 95.1 seconds). Each item was generated five times with independent random sampling.

To exclude likely generation failures, pairs are excluded if either model produces an empty output or audio outside the specified duration range.

### Japanese Reading — Joyo Kanji Yomi Benchmark: Parakeet Edition

We used [JKYB-Parakeet](https://github.com/Parakeet-Inc/Joyo-Kanji-Yomi-Benchmark-Parakeet-Edition), with 13,536 texts × 5 repeats, without reference audio or captions. We treated outputs lasting 1–10 seconds as successful generations and retained pairs where both models met this criterion (66,423 / 67,680 pairs).

| Model | Target Reading Accuracy ↑ | Kana-CER ↓ | Kana-CER clipped ↓ | Sentence Kana-CER ↓ | Standard Text CER ↓ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Fish Audio Drama 3 | 92.021% | 7.474% | 6.285% | **1.421%** | 5.699% |
| Drama-3-Japanese | **93.188%** | **6.548%** | **5.511%** | 2.087% | **5.572%** |

Scores are pooled across five runs using the official Parakeet Edition evaluator.

### Voice Cloning — JVS

We evaluated 100 JVS speakers × 5 texts × 5 repeats, with one or three reference clips and no captions. Both models used the same references and transcripts.

We treated outputs lasting 1–20 seconds as successful generations and retained pairs where both models met this criterion (2,492 / 2,500 pairs with one reference and 2,429 / 2,500 pairs with three references).

| Model | References | CAM++ Similarity ↑ | ERes2Net Similarity ↑ | CAM++ Top-1 ↑ | ERes2Net Top-1 ↑ | Whisper CER ↓ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Fish Audio Drama 3 | 1 | **0.7333** | **0.6988** | **97.43%** | 95.83% | **2.886%** |
| Drama-3-Japanese | 1 | 0.7280 | 0.6919 | 97.11% | **96.67%** | 3.082% |
| Fish Audio Drama 3 | 3 | **0.7769** | **0.7402** | **99.75%** | **99.71%** | 3.023% |
| Drama-3-Japanese | 3 | 0.7688 | 0.7336 | 99.30% | 99.42% | **3.008%** |

Scores are means across five repeats. The evaluation follows the [Irodori-TTS voice cloning benchmark procedure](https://huggingface.co/Aratako/Irodori-TTS-v4-Small/blob/main/VOICE_CLONING_BENCHMARK.md), adapted to compare one versus three reference clips.

## ⚠️ Limitations

- **Japanese-only fine-tuning:** Performance in other languages has not been evaluated.
- **Single-speaker TTS:** Fine-tuning covers single-speaker utterances, not multi-speaker conversations, audio editing, multi-turn dialogue, or director's notes.
- **Up to three references:** Fine-tuning used at most three same-speaker reference clips. Larger reference sets are outside the training setup.
- **Generation stability:** As with the base model, generation may stop mid-sentence, include long periods of silence, or occasionally produce no audio.
- **Caption and tag control:** Instructions may be applied inconsistently, especially when reference speech, captions, and tags conflict. Automatically annotated training tags can also contain errors.

## 📜 License

This model inherits the [Fish Audio Community License, Version 1.0](LICENSE) from original model.

## 🙏 Acknowledgments

- [Fish Audio](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) for Drama 3, the codec, and the official inference implementation.
- [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) for benchmark inference.

Special thanks to [gabrielclark3330](https://huggingface.co/gabrielclark3330) and [kikouousya](https://huggingface.co/kikouousya) for supporting this project.

The public Darwin reference is [FINAL-Bench/Darwin-TTS-1.7B-Cross](https://huggingface.co/FINAL-Bench/Darwin-TTS-1.7B-Cross), whose documented construction blends the Qwen3-TTS Base and Qwen3-1.7B LLM branches in weight space. | | 7 | **NOESIS language expansion** | Family-specific LoRA/GRPO/DPO training and routing expanded the tested NOESIS surface to **112 languages**. One family adapter is selected per request; adapters are never summed into a single destructive checkpoint. | The five 1.7B branches above must not be confused with five independent public Qwen repositories: the original Qwen Base, LLM and ASR checkpoints are public links; Talker/Combo are the speech and derived cross-modal branches represented by the Qwen3-TTS/Darwin lineage and this NOESIS artifact. The model card keeps this distinction explicit for reproducibility and attribution. ### Language and test accounting The canonical NOESIS claim for this bundle is **112 languages tested end-to-end (112/112)**. The 95-code family-adapter table below is a routing table for the documented family adapters, not the complete count of the NOESIS test surface. The legacy file named `manifest_94.json` is a partial adapter-sweep manifest and must not be interpreted as the total language coverage. The upstream Qwen3-TTS codec itself has 10 native language IDs; the remaining languages use the NOESIS family, sibling, or generic route selected by the production router. ## What is in the bundle ```text NOESIS-Qwen3-TTS-1.7B-Talker-Combo-LLM2-ASR2-BF16/ ├── README.md ├── LICENSE ├── model.safetensors # NOESIS-Qwen3-TTS-1.7B-Talker-Combo-LLM2-ASR2-BF16 ├── config.json ├── generation_config.json ├── tokenizer_config.json ├── vocab.json / merges.txt ├── speech_tokenizer/ # Qwen3-TTS audio tokenizer assets ├── adapters/ # one family adapter at a time └── test_audio_perfamily/ # evaluation references and manifests ``` The deprecated attempt to sum all eleven adapters into one merged checkpoint is **not** the production model. Merging unrelated family adapters destroyed EOS and codec behavior and produced long non-speech outputs. Always load the Combo base and select exactly one family adapter when a non-native route is required. ## Language → family adapter | Family | Adapter directory | Languages | |---|---|---| | `germanic` | `adapters/NOESIS-Talker-Combo-germanic-LoRA-r8-BF16` | `en`, `de`, `nl`, `sv`, `da`, `nb`, `is`, `af` | | `romance` | `adapters/…-romance-…` | `es`, `fr`, `it`, `pt`, `ro`, `ca`, `gl`, `oc` | | `slavic` | `adapters/…-slavic-…` | `ru`, `uk`, `pl`, `cs`, `sk`, `sl`, `hr`, `sr`, `bg`, `mk`, `be` | | `sinitic` | `adapters/…-sinitic-…` | `zh`, `yue` | | `other_eurasian` | `adapters/…-other_eurasian-…` | `ja`, `ko`, `mn`, `hy`, `ka`, `fi`, `hu`, `et`, `lv`, `lt`, `el`, `eu` | | `semitic` | `adapters/…-semitic-…` | `ar`, `he`, `mt`, `am`, `ti` | | `indic` | `adapters/…-indic-…` | `hi`, `bn`, `mr`, `ta`, `te`, `pa`, `ur`, `gu`, `kn`, `ml`, `or`, `as`, `ne` | | `turkic` | `adapters/…-turkic-…` | `tr`, `uz`, `kk`, `az`, `ky`, `tk`, `ug` | | `iranian` | `adapters/…-iranian-…` | `fa`, `ps`, `tg`, `ckb`, `kmr` | | `nigero_congo` | `adapters/…-nigero_congo-…` | `sw`, `ha`, `yo`, `zu`, `ig`, `xh`, `sn`, `ny`, `lg`, `om`, `so`, `wo`, `kam`, `ln`, `luo`, `rw` | | `austronesian` | `adapters/…-austronesian-…` | `id`, `ms`, `vi`, `th`, `fil`, `jv`, `mi`, `ceb` | The ten native Qwen3-TTS languages -- `en`, `ru`, `zh`, `de`, `fr`, `es`, `ja`, `ko`, `it`, and `pt` -- normally use plain Combo without a family adapter. Arabic (`ar`) is routed through the semitic family adapter in this bundle. Other languages select the matching family, sibling, or generic route. The production router performs this mapping automatically. ### r16 adapter update The `indic` and `iranian` families have r16 variants and should use them when the directory is present. The router falls back to r8 if an r16 directory is unavailable. The `semitic` family remains on r8. Several Brahmic Indic languages—especially `te`, `pa`, `ml`, `or`, and `kn`—showed EOS overgeneration in the current sweep; increasing rank alone does not fix that behavior. They require a dedicated training and EOS-fix pass rather than repeated re-generation. ## Quality status The complete NOESIS test program covered **all 112 languages (112/112 tested)**. The dated per-family adapter sweep is a subset of that program: its legacy `manifest_94.json` records 86 scored checks plus six no-FLEURS skips and is not a total-coverage manifest. The full 112-language result is the canonical coverage claim; each route must still pass the normal NOESIS ASR, speaker-similarity, emotion, and timing gates before production acceptance. | Status | Guidance | |---|---| | Strong families | Romance, Slavic, Germanic, Austronesian, Other Eurasian, and Sinitic were the most consistent in the recorded sweep. | | Low-resource / ASR-gap languages | `am`, `as`, `ckb`, `ha`, `he`, `hy`, `ig`, `kam`, `ky`, `luo`, `nb`, `ps`, `so`, `ta`, `tg`, `yo` need native listening checks because generic ASR scores can under-report quality. | | EOS overgeneration | `te`, `pa`, `ml`, `or`, and `kn` can run to the token cap without a valid EOS and must not be accepted without a successful quality gate. | | Production decision | Use the router and keep the 0.6B OmniVoice bundle as the primary generic clone engine; use Combo as the designated fallback or language route. | ## How to run in NOESIS production There is intentionally no `run.bat` in this model directory. Do not launch the safetensors file directly. The supported route is the parent NOESIS runtime: ```text NOESIS-3.5B-A0.5B-DUBBING-FILM/ ├── demo_server/_voice_swap_runner.py # router / subprocess orchestration ├── NOESIS-Qwen3-Omni-MoE-BF16/ │ ├── _qwen_tts_worker.py # resident JSON-IPC worker │ └── NOESIS-Qwen3-TTS-1.7B-Talker-Combo-LLM2-ASR2-BF16/ │ ├── model.safetensors │ └── adapters/ └── dubbing/ # timing and quality pipeline ``` The worker runs inside the frozen `_venv_qwen_tts_457` environment. On Windows, its subprocess must inherit `PYTHONUTF8=1` and `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`; otherwise non-ASCII text can corrupt the JSON IPC stream. A production request contains the target text, the reference audio or speaker embedding, the target language, the selected family adapter, and the adapter scale: ```json { "op": "clone", "text": "Welcome to the Sanctuary, Miss Amelia.", "target_lang": "en", "adapter": "germanic", "adapter_scale": 0.32 } ``` The exact worker schema is owned by the parent router and may add reference-audio, x-vector, duration, and cache fields. The adapter policy does not change: **one family adapter, one scale, one active Talker route**. Do not send all family adapters in one request. ### Typical Windows environment ```bat cd /d B:\Downloads\Portable\NOESIS-VC-ONE\models\llm\NOESIS-3.5B-A0.5B-DUBBING-FILM set PYTHONUTF8=1 set PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 set NOESIS_TTS_PRIMARY=combo REM The parent production server starts the resident worker and routes requests. REM Start it using the bundle's normal demo_server launcher; do not run the REM model.safetensors file as a Python script. ``` `NOESIS_TTS_PRIMARY=combo` is an explicit fallback selection. The default generic production route is OmniVoice (`omni06`); set the variable only when testing or intentionally routing through Combo. ## Direct model-loading outline For development and diagnostics, load the base and one adapter through the Qwen3-TTS/PEFT runtime used by the parent worker. The following is an outline of the required policy, not a replacement for the pinned worker implementation: ```python # Pseudocode: use the parent worker's pinned loader and tokenizer setup. base = load_qwen3_tts("NOESIS-Qwen3-TTS-1.7B-Talker-Combo-LLM2-ASR2-BF16") base.load_lora("adapters/NOESIS-Talker-Combo-romance-LoRA-r8-BF16") base.set_lora_scale(0.32) waveform = base.generate_voice_clone( text="Bonjour, bienvenue au Sanctuaire.", reference_audio="clean_reference.wav", language="fr", ) base.unload_lora() ``` The parent worker also handles CUDA placement, reference-text or x-vector requirements, output normalization, caching, and cleanup. multilingual - voice-cloning - voice-design library_name: omnivoice --- # OmniVoice 🌍

         

OmniVoice is a massively multilingual zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) model supporting over 600 languages. Built on a novel diffusion language model-style architecture, it delivers high-quality speech with superior inference speed, supporting voice cloning and voice design. - **Paper:** [OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models](https://huggingface.co/papers/2604.00688) - **Repository:** [GitHub](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) - **Demo:** [Hugging Face Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) - **Colab:** [Google Colab Notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/k2-fsa/OmniVoice/blob/master/docs/OmniVoice.ipynb) ## Key Features - **600+ Languages Supported**: The broadest language coverage among zero-shot TTS models. - **Voice Cloning**: State-of-the-art voice cloning quality from a short reference audio. - **Voice Design**: Control voices via assigned speaker attributes (gender, age, pitch, dialect/accent, whisper, etc.). - **Fine-grained Control**: Non-verbal symbols (e.g., `[laughter]`) and pronunciation correction via pinyin or phonemes. - **Fast Inference**: RTF as low as 0.025 (40x faster than real-time). - **Diffusion Language Model-style Architecture**: A clean, streamlined, and scalable design that delivers both quality and speed. ## Usage To get started, install the `omnivoice` library: > We recommend using a fresh virtual environment (e.g., `conda`, `venv`, etc.) to avoid conflicts. **Step 1**: Install PyTorch
NVIDIA GPU ```bash # Install pytorch with your CUDA version, e.g. pip install torch==2.8.0+cu128 torchaudio==2.8.0+cu128 --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 ``` > See [PyTorch official site](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/) for other versions installation.
Apple Silicon ```bash pip install torch==2.8.0 torchaudio==2.8.0 ```
**Step 2**: Install OmniVoice ```bash pip install omnivoice ``` ### Python API You can use OmniVoice for zero-shot voice cloning as follows: ```python from omnivoice import OmniVoice import soundfile as sf import torch # Load the model model = OmniVoice.from_pretrained( "k2-fsa/OmniVoice", device_map="cuda:0", dtype=torch.float16 ) # Generate audio audio = model.generate( text="Hello, this is a test of zero-shot voice cloning.", ref_audio="ref.wav", ref_text="Transcription of the reference audio.", ) # audio is a list of `np.ndarray` with shape (T,) at 24 kHz. sf.write("out.wav", audio[0], 24000) ``` For more generation modes (e.g., voice design), functions (e.g., non-verbal symbols, pronunciation correction) and comprehensive usage instructions, see our [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice). ## Discussion & Communication You can directly discuss on [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice/issues). You can also scan the QR code to join our wechat group or follow our wechat official account. | Wechat Group | Wechat Official Account | | ------------ | ----------------------- | |![wechat](https://k2-fsa.org/zh-CN/assets/pic/wechat_group.jpg) |![wechat](https://k2-fsa.org/zh-CN/assets/pic/wechat_account.jpg) | ## Citation ```bibtex @article{zhu2026omnivoice, title={OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models}, author={Zhu, Han and Ye, Lingxuan and Kang, Wei and Yao, Zengwei and Guo, Liyong and Kuang, Fangjun and Han, Zhifeng and Zhuang, Weiji and Lin, Long and Povey, Daniel}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.00688}, year={2026} } ``` ## License Our code is released under the Apache 2.0 License. Lure 0.6B

Expressive voice cloning in 0.6B parameters. It laughs, sighs, breaks and whispers where you tell it to.
Research preview · English · 0.6B parameters · 24 kHz · Lure Turbo · lure-tts engine

> [!WARNING] > **Research preview.** Weights, behaviour and this card can change between releases. Pin a revision if you build on it. ## Overview Lure is a 0.6B text-to-speech model for English. Give it a few seconds of a voice and the transcript of that clip, and it reads new text in that voice. Put a sound inline, like `(laugh)` or `(sharp inhale)`, and it performs the sound at that spot instead of reading the word. Add a short acting note, like `"Hushed and shaking, close to tears."`, and it plays the line that way. Most open models in its class are 1.5B to 35B parameters. On the public English benchmarks below, Lure's word accuracy sits alongside models three to sixty times its size, and its naturalness score (UTMOS) is the highest in the table. It runs faster than real time on a MacBook, and a single L4 streams 8 voices at once. **Lure Turbo** is the same voice with a faster decoding head: it predicts the 15 fine audio codes of each frame in 3 passes instead of 15, which makes the per-frame decode step about 3.4x faster with no measurable loss on any benchmark. See [Speed](#speed). | | | |---|---| | **Parameters** | 0.6B | | **Language** | English only | | **Output** | 24 kHz mono, streaming | | **Codec** | 12.5 Hz, 16 codebooks (Qwen3-TTS 12Hz format) | | **Cloning** | zero-shot, 3 to 12 s reference plus its transcript | | **Sounds** | inline tags in round brackets, 36 supported | | **Direction** | optional free-text acting note | ## Speed Lure streams audio while it generates. RTF is generation time divided by audio length (lower is faster); TTFA is the time to the first audio chunk. Measured with the [lure-tts](https://github.com/smirki/lure-tts) engine, cuda backend, bf16. **H100** | Model | Streams | TTFA | ms per frame | RTF | |---|---|---|---|---| | Lure | 1 | 283 ms | 18.4 | 0.23 | | Lure | 8 | 331 ms | 19.6 | 0.25 | | Lure Turbo | 1 | **168 ms** | **11.4** | **0.14** | | Lure Turbo | 8 | 200 ms | 12.4 | 0.15 | With a smaller first chunk, Lure Turbo reaches 135 ms median time to first audio on the H100. **L4 (24 GB)** | Model | 1 stream | 8 streams, total | |---|---|---| | Lure | 28.8 frames/s (2.3x real time) | 219 frames/s (17x real time) | | Lure Turbo | **50.6 frames/s (4.0x real time)** | **374 frames/s (30x real time)** | ## Benchmarks

Lure and Lure Turbo were run with each benchmark's official scripts, one take per line, default sampling. Other rows are the numbers their developers published. Best value in each column in bold. | Model | Size | Seed-TTS WER ↓ | Seed-TTS SIM ↑ | LibriSpeech-PC SIM ↑ | LibriSpeech-PC UTMOS ↑ | VDB SIM ↑ | CV3 emotion % ↑ | RTF ↓ | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Lure** | 0.6B | 1.51 | 0.653 | 0.638 | **4.43** | **0.81** | 73.3 | 0.230 | | **Lure Turbo** | 0.6B | 1.59 | 0.654 | 0.641 | 4.38 | **0.81** | 73.3 | 0.140 | | Fish S2 Pro | 5B | **0.99** | – | – | – | – | – | 0.195 | | Qwen3-TTS 0.6B | 0.6B | 1.32 | – | – | – | – | – | – | | Fish Drama 3 | 35B MoE | 1.54 | 0.640 | 0.605 | 4.31 | – | – | **0.131** | | Ming 3.0 0.5B | ~1B | 1.58 | 0.691 | – | – | – | – | – | | FireRedTTS3 | 1.7B+ | 1.64 | **0.772** | – | – | – | – | – | | VoxCPM2 | 2B | 1.84 | 0.753 | – | – | 0.70 | – | – | | F5-TTS | – | 2.00 | 0.670 | – | – | – | 64.7 | – | | CosyVoice3 | – | 2.22 | 0.720 | 0.694 | 4.28 | – | – | – | | dots.tts | 2B | – | 0.770 | – | – | – | – | – | | Ming Tiny | 7.9B MoE | – | 0.728 | – | – | – | 74.0 | – | | IndexTTS2 | 1.5B | – | 0.706 | – | – | – | – | – | | OmniVoice | 0.6B | – | – | **0.729** | 4.28 | – | – | – | | Qwen3-TTS | 0.6B-1.7B | – | – | 0.704 | 4.41 | – | – | – | | Real recordings | – | – | – | – | 4.10 | – | – | – | | Inworld TTS-2 | – | – | – | – | – | 0.71 | – | – | | Breeze TTS 2 | 3B | – | – | – | – | 0.67 | – | 0.320 | | MiMo-v2.5 | – | – | – | – | – | 0.66 | – | – | | Qwen-Audio 3.0+ | – | – | – | – | – | 0.65 | – | – | | StepAudio 2.5 | – | – | – | – | – | 0.64 | – | – | | CosyVoice3 1.5B +DiffRO-EMO | 1.5B | – | – | – | – | – | **77.7** | – | | Ming 0.5B | ~1B | – | – | – | – | – | 72.3 | – | | CosyVoice3 0.5B | 0.5B | – | – | – | – | – | 66.3 | – | | CosyVoice3 1.5B | 1.5B | – | – | – | – | – | 63.0 | – | | Higgs TTS 3 | 4B | – | – | – | – | – | – | 0.147 | Notes: - **Fish Drama 3** regenerates flagged takes for its 1.54 Seed-TTS WER; its first-take WER is 2.20. Its LibriSpeech-PC similarity is 0.605 with one reference clip and 0.633 with three. Lure's numbers are first takes: the same flagged-take check found nothing to regenerate. - **LibriSpeech-PC**: other models use the OmniVoice scoring setup as quoted in the Fish Drama 3 report; Lure uses the F5-TTS scripts. Real recordings score UTMOS 4.10 and similarity 0.695 under the same scripts. - **Voice Direction Benchmark (VDB)**: the column is speaker similarity while following directions. Lure holds the reference voice closely, partly because it rarely changes accent, age or gender when asked; its direction score is 2.42 / 5. - **CV3-Eval**: emotion2vec labels mapped by name (the official script's label order is out of date). - **RTF**: Lure on H100; Fish models were measured on H200. - **Size**: whole checkpoint as published; MoE models show total parameters. Closed models publish no size. ## Quick start ### lure-tts (recommended: streaming, Turbo, Mac / NVIDIA / CPU) ```bash git clone https://github.com/smirki/lure-tts && cd lure-tts hf download smirki/lure-tts-0.6b-preview --local-dir models/lure pip install ./backends/mlx ".[server]" # Mac; see the repo for NVIDIA and the C++ build ``` ```python from lure_tts import Lure tts = Lure.load("models/lure") voice = tts.make_voice("reference.wav", "Transcript of the reference clip.", name="me") tts.speak("Wait, you're staying? (sharp inhale) Since when?", voice, instruct="Sudden, bright shock, then a caught breath.", out="out.wav") for pcm in tts.stream("(sigh) Fine. I'm in.", "me"): # float32 chunks at 24 kHz ... ``` `lure serve` starts an OpenAI-compatible speech server (`POST /v1/audio/speech`) that batches concurrent requests. ### qwen-tts (PyTorch) Lure uses the Qwen3-TTS 12Hz format, so the `qwen-tts` package loads it directly (without Turbo): ```python import soundfile as sf from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel tts = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("smirki/lure-tts-0.6b-preview", device_map="cuda:0", dtype="bfloat16") wavs, sr = tts.generate_voice_clone( text="I'm sorry. (sigh) I never meant for any of this to happen.", language="English", ref_audio="reference.wav", ref_text="Transcript of the reference clip.", non_streaming_mode=True, ) sf.write("out.wav", wavs[0], sr) ``` `qwen-tts` turns the direction (instruct) off for 0.6B models; use lure-tts if you want directions. ## Sound tags Write tags in round brackets, lowercase, at the spot where the sound should happen: `I can't believe it (laugh) you actually did it.` Square brackets like `[laugh]` are not supported. | Group | Tags | |---|---| | Laughter | `(laugh)` `(chuckle)` `(giggle)` `(nervous laugh)` `(wheezing laugh)` `(laughs while talking)` | | Breath | `(sigh)` `(frustrated sigh)` `(relieved sigh)` `(exhale)` `(inhale)` `(sharp inhale)` `(gasp)` `(happy gasp)` `(yawn)` | | Crying | `(voice breaking)` `(sob)` `(whimper)` `(sniff)` `(sniffle)` | | Throat and mouth | `(cough)` `(clears throat)` `(swallow)` `(gulp)` `(lip smack)` `(tsk)` `(snort)` `(grunt)` `(groan)` `(hum)` | | Spoken sounds | `(hmm)` `(ugh)` `(pfft)` `(scoff)` `(ow)` | | Timing | `(pause)` | - Laughs, sighs, gasps and sharp inhales are the most reliable. Rarer tags like `(ow)` or `(sob)` land less often. - One or two tags per sentence works best. - If a take misses a tag, regenerate with a new seed. ## Direction A direction is a short note to the actor: emotion, pace, pitch, breath. It is optional; without one, Lure reads the delivery from the words and tags. - `Sudden, bright shock. Fast attack on the question, then a caught breath lifting pitch sharply upward.` - `Slow, stunned, hushed. Barely any pitch movement, like the brain is still buffering.` - `Tight, shivering disbelief. Thin voice, trembly pitch, the laugh escaping between clauses.` ## Recommended settings | Setting | Value | |---|---| | Language | `english` (always set it; `auto` uses a different prompt and hurts quality) | | Sampling | temperature 0.9, top-k 50, top-p 1.0, repetition penalty 1.05, same for the sub-talker | | Precision | bf16 | | Prompt layout | non-streaming (full text up front); lure-tts does this automatically | | Reference clip | 3 to 12 s, one speaker, clean, no music. The output inherits the clip's mic and room. | | Reference transcript | The exact words in the clip. A wrong transcript causes skipped or repeated words. | | Text per call | A sentence or short paragraph. For long text, split on sentences (lure-tts does this and streams each piece). | | Retry rule | If a take runs past twice its expected length or never stops, regenerate with a new seed. | ## Limitations - English only. Other languages have not been tested. - Directions shape emotion and pace well, but Lure is weaker than large instruction-tuned models at changing who is speaking (accent, age, gender) on request. - Sound tags are best effort; a take sometimes skips one. - Very long single calls can stop early or drift in voice. Split long text into sentences. - Do not use Lure to imitate a real person without their consent. Training data includes YODAS v3.

# TangYuGe GPT-SoVITS v2ProPlus

Fine-tuned [GPT-SoVITS](https://github.com/RVC-Boss/GPT-SoVITS) **v2ProPlus** weights for the voice of *Tang Yuge (唐语歌)*, a character from the visual novel *Sparkling Memories (夏日花火)*. Chinese (Mandarin) only, 32 kHz mono output.

This repository is self-contained: fine-tuned GPT and SoVITS weights, 19 scene profiles with their reference clips and prompt texts, inference / HTTP-bridge scripts, and (optionally) every auxiliary and base model needed to run or continue training. Current release: **GPT `G-F2+DPO` epoch 10 + SoVITS epoch 4** (`weights/tangyuge_v2pp_dpo-e10.ckpt`, `weights/tangyuge_v2pp_e4_s564.pth`).

## Model Details

### Model Description

- **Maintainer:** shiqianyan
- **Model type:** two-stage autoregressive TTS. A GPT (text → semantic tokens) and a SoVITS (semantic tokens + reference → waveform), both fully fine-tuned (not LoRA) from the official v2ProPlus base models.
- **Language:** Mandarin Chinese
- **Fine-tuned from:** [`lj1995/GPT-SoVITS`](https://huggingface.co/lj1995/GPT-SoVITS) (`s1v3.ckpt`, `v2Pro/s2Gv2ProPlus.pth`, `v2Pro/s2Dv2ProPlus.pth`)
- **Sources:** training code is the official GPT-SoVITS (commit `ea2d2a8`); only the learning-rate schedule launcher and a switch for the official DPO option were added (see [Training Procedure](#training-procedure)).

## Uses

### Direct use

Generating Chinese dialogue in this character's voice for fan works, game mods, character chat bots and personal study or research. Pick a scene profile that matches the tone of the line (see [Scene profiles](#scene-profiles)); the reference clip and its prompt text control emotion and rhythm to a large degree.

### Out-of-scope use

Non-Chinese text; mixed Chinese–English text (untested); anything that needs the original actor's exact performance; impersonating a real person; misleading or unlawful use. Please label generated audio as AI-synthesised.

## Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- **Short utterances** can end early (e.g. only the first half of a four-syllable line is spoken). This is a known property of GPT-SoVITS autoregressive decoding; the conservative sampling defaults below reduce it but cannot rule it out.
- **Electronic / "muffled" artefacts.** Some outputs, especially with the serious reference (`serious_script41_L0682`, the default of `main_hybrid_mid`), have light electronic distortion or a "mouth full" quality. These artefacts are present in the shipped SoVITS epoch 4 and were **not** fixed by any later experiment. Automatic metrics (DNSMOS, ASR error rate) do not detect them, so no improvement is claimed.
- **Non-speech sounds** (laughter, breaths, sighs) have no dedicated tokens in GPT-SoVITS (the phoneme vocabulary is full). They only emerge when the text contains interjections such as 嘻嘻 / 哈哈 / 唉, and quality is below natural laughter. In our test, about three quarters of the expected event types were realised (event recall 0.77, see [Evaluation](#evaluation)).
- Reference clip and **prompt text must be paired**. A wrong prompt text noticeably degrades pronunciation and rhythm.
- Voice and timbre are limited by about 43 minutes of source recordings; strong emotion (shouting, crying) is weak.
- On some Intel hybrid-architecture CPUs (reproduced on i7-13650HX) PyTorch's oneDNN multi-threaded `Conv1d` returns wrong results. GPU inference is unaffected; for CPU, set `torch.backends.mkldnn.enabled = False` or run single-threaded.
- Part of the GPT training data is synthetic speech from a commercial TTS service imitating the same character. It is not redistributed here, and it can propagate that service's own mispronunciations.

### Recommendations

Keep the default sampling parameters, use the scene profile closest to the text, listen to the output before publishing, and do not use it to imitate real people.

## How to Get Started

### 1. Prepare GPT-SoVITS

```bash
git clone https://github.com/RVC-Boss/GPT-SoVITS.git
cd GPT-SoVITS && git checkout ea2d2a8      # install its Python dependencies as documented upstream
```

### 2. Download this repository

Put it next to `GPT-SoVITS/`:

```bash
cd .. && hf download shiqianyan/TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus --local-dir TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus
```

If you already run GPT-SoVITS v2ProPlus and have its auxiliary models (BERT, HuBERT, SV, G2PW, fast_langdetect), you only need the weights, profiles, references and scripts; skip the large overlay:

```bash
hf download shiqianyan/TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus --exclude "GPT-SoVITS-overlay/*" --local-dir TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus
```

### 3. Install the auxiliary models (unless you already have them)

```bash
python TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus/scripts/install_pretrained.py --gptsovits-root GPT-SoVITS
```

The script verifies hashes and copies `GPT-SoVITS-overlay/` into the GPT-SoVITS tree (existing identical files are skipped). The overlay contains two groups:

| Group | Files | Needed for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auxiliary models | `chinese-roberta-wwm-ext-large` (BERT), `chinese-hubert-base`, `sv/` (speaker verification), `text/G2PWModel`, `fast_langdetect` | **Inference** |
| Official v2ProPlus base models | `v2Pro/s2Gv2ProPlus.pth`, `v2Pro/s2Dv2ProPlus.pth`, `s1v3.ckpt` | Continued training only |

The fine-tuned weights are complete inference models. GPT-SoVITS drops the posterior encoder (`enc_q`) and the discriminator when saving, so continuing training from them needs the base models to restore those parts.

### 4. Synthesize

Use the GPT-SoVITS Python environment:

```bash
# default profile (serious / long lines)
python TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus/scripts/run_tangyuge_infer.py --text "这里填写要合成的中文文本。" --output output.wav

# another scene: switch the profile
python TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus/scripts/run_tangyuge_infer.py \
  --voice-profile TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus/profiles/morning.yaml \
  --text "早上好呀，今天也要元气满满哦。" --output morning.wav
```

Add `--gptsovits-root <path>` if the two directories are not siblings, and `--seed N` for reproducibility.

### 5. HTTP service (optional)

```bash
python TangYuGe-GPT-SoVITS-v2ProPlus/scripts/start_tangyuge_bridge.py
```

This serves `/tts` on `127.0.0.1:9881` (the GPT-SoVITS `api_v2` backend runs on `9880`). The bridge picks a scene from the text, or you can name one:

```python
import requests

r = requests.post(
    "http://127.0.0.1:9881/tts",
    json={"text": "早上好呀，今天也要元气满满哦。", "profile": "morning"},   # "profile" is optional
    timeout=120,
)
open("output.wav", "wb").write(r.content)
```

Request fields: `text` (required), `profile` / `scene` / `reference` (choose a scene), `top_k`, `top_p`, `temperature`, and the usual `api_v2` fields. Helper endpoints: `GET /health`, `GET /profiles`, `GET /references`.

If you call the plain GPT-SoVITS `api_v2` backend yourself, the weights are fixed by the server, but **every request must still carry the scene's reference clip and its prompt text** (from `manifests/references.yaml`):

```json
{
  "text": "早上好呀，今天也要元气满满哦。",
  "text_lang": "zh",
  "ref_audio_path": "<repo>/references/morning_script43_L0993.wav",
  "prompt_text": "曦铭？这么早就来学校了呀。",
  "prompt_lang": "zh",
  "top_k": 5, "top_p": 0.8, "temperature": 0.7,
  "text_split_method": "cut5", "batch_size": 1,
  "media_type": "wav", "streaming_mode": false
}
```

Each profile binds weights, config, reference clip and prompt text with relative paths, so the repository can be moved anywhere:

```yaml

weights:
  gpt: ../weights/tangyuge_v2pp_dpo-e10.ckpt
  sovits: ../weights/tangyuge_v2pp_e4_s564.pth

  reference_id: serious_script41_L0682
  ref_audio_path: ../references/serious_script41_L0682.wav
```

## Training Details

### Training data

All voice data come from the character's in-game lines (702 clips, about 48.8 min, extracted from the game); the dataset itself is **not** released. Transcripts were checked with ASR: no obviously wrong labels (mean pinyin error 2.0%, none above 30%).

| Stage | Data |
| --- | --- |
| SoVITS | 561 real clips (1–12 s, at least 6 Chinese characters), about 43.1 min |
| GPT | 1559 clips: **685 real** (the 561 above + 124 short / interjection lines that the length and character-count rules had dropped; used for GPT only), **845 synthetic** (about 57.5 min; speech from a commercial TTS service imitating the same voice, filtered as below), and **29 duplicated** real clips that contain 我们 |

Synthetic-data filtering (all machine gates): duration 1–12 s, clipping ≤ 1%, pinyin edit distance to the text ≤ 1 (0 for lines of up to 4 syllables) with coverage ≥ 0.9 on a local Paraformer transcript, DNSMOS background score ≥ 3.5, and for laughter lines the event tag must appear in a speech-to-text transcript with event tags. Clips containing 我们 were removed from the synthetic part (their articulation did not match the real voice), and 5 clips the maintainer found unnatural were removed by ear.

### Training Procedure

**SoVITS** (unchanged from the first release): started from `s2Gv2ProPlus.pth` / `s2Dv2ProPlus.pth`, batch size 4, learning rate 1e-4, fp16, 8 epochs saved, epoch 4 (step 564) selected.

**GPT** (this release): started from the official `s1v3.ckpt`, official training script and optimizer (ScaledAdam, optimizer step every 4 batches), batch size 4, 16-bit mixed precision, 10 epochs, one checkpoint per epoch.

- *Learning rate.* The upstream code pins the GPT learning rate to a constant 0.002, so each saved epoch is a snapshot taken at a high learning rate and pinyin error rate swings from epoch to epoch (1.5–4.7% in our runs). We replaced only the scheduler, with a launcher that leaves the GPT-SoVITS source untouched (`scripts/s1_train_annealed.py`, total updates set through the `S1_TOTAL_UPDATES` environment variable): linear warm-up (1e-5 → 2e-3 over 50 optimizer updates) then cosine decay to 1e-4. With the schedule the epoch-to-epoch swing dropped to 1.25–1.63%.
- *DPO.* The official "DPO training (experimental)" option (`train.if_dpo: true` in the s1 config) adds a preference loss (β = 0.2, reference-free) in which, for every batch, a "rejected" semantic sequence is built by repeating a random segment or deleting one, so the model learns to move away from repeated and swallowed syllables.
- *Observation.* In the DPO run the logged step count was twice that of the non-DPO runs (7769 vs 3889) and the learning rate hit its floor at about epoch 6 instead of epoch 10, because the total update count (970) had been set for the non-DPO run. Epochs 7–10 therefore ran at the minimum learning rate of 1e-4. We did not test a re-scaled schedule.

Variants compared (all from `s1v3.ckpt`): `F` / `F2` (constant LR, 14 epochs; F2 drops synthetic 我们 clips), `G-F` / `G-F2` (same data, annealed LR, 10 epochs), and **`G-F2+DPO`** (G-F2 plus official DPO, 10 epochs) which is released.

## Evaluation

### Protocol

Candidates are compared with a baseline on the same sentence, same reference clip and same random seed, and every figure is a paired difference with a 95% interval from a bootstrap over sentences.

- **Test sentences:** 100 sentences that are not in the training data (checked against the script); 12 extra lines (6 laughter, 6 interjection); and, for the final check, **59 further unseen sentences** (checked against the training script and all earlier test sentences, with extra laughter, sigh and emotion lines).
- **References:** two real-voice scene references (`serious_script41_L0682`, `question_clear_script34_L0420`); 1–3 seeds per sentence depending on the test set.
- **Metrics**
  - *Pinyin error rate (PER):* toneless pinyin edit distance between the target text and a local Paraformer-large transcript; laughter lines excluded. *Severe-error rate:* share of utterances with PER > 10%.
  - *Speaker similarity:* cosine similarity of ERes2NetV2 embeddings against the real recordings.
  - *DNSMOS (P.835):* SIG (speech distortion), BAK (background noise); *noise floor:* 10th-percentile RMS of non-silent frames (dB).
  - *Event recall:* for sentences where a same-text reference rendition contains non-speech events (laughter, breath, sigh), the share of those event types that a tag-emitting speech-to-text service finds in our output (13–16 such sentences, one reference).
  - *Prosody closeness:* correlation of log-F0 and energy contours plus speaking-rate ratio against that reference rendition (weak at separating systems; versions differ by about 0.01).
- **Composite score and gates** (used to select checkpoints): speaker similarity 35%, emotion / non-speech events 25%, articulation 25%, cleanliness 15%. Each paired difference is mapped linearly to 0–100 (50 = same as baseline). Three gates are applied first: speaker similarity not lower by more than 0.01, PER not higher by more than 0.3 pp, severe errors not higher by more than 1.5 pp.

### Results

Final comparison, 59 unseen sentences × 2 references × 3 seeds (354 utterances per system):

| Metric | e14 (first release) | d2 (previous release) | **This release** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pinyin error rate (laughter lines excluded) | 4.42% | 2.41% | 2.53% |
| Severe-error rate (PER > 10%) | 13.0% | 10.3% | 11.0% |
| Event recall (laugh / breath / sigh) | 0.67 | 0.58 | **0.77** |
| Speaker similarity | 0.884 | 0.886 | 0.885 |
| DNSMOS SIG / BAK | 3.13 / 3.66 | 3.10 / 3.61 | 3.12 / 3.58 |
| Noise floor (dB) | −57.2 | −56.7 | −56.6 |

![Release comparison](assets/04_final_vs_previous.png)

Composite score with all test data pooled: **57.4** vs d2 (95% interval 48.2–67.3; 119 sentences, 474 pairs) and **66.8** vs e14 (51.4–73.6; 159 sentences, 554 pairs); all three gates pass.

**How to read this.** Articulation, timbre and cleanliness are on par with d2; the clear difference is that laughter / breath / sigh cues are realised about 0.2 more often. Intervals overlap for every metric, so this is "not worse and better at non-speech events", not a statistically significant across-the-board gain. Absolute PER depends heavily on the sentence set (short interjection lines are hard) and cannot be compared with earlier reports on other sets.

Per-epoch behaviour (100 sentences × 2 references, one seed, versus e14):

![Per-epoch comparison](assets/03_gpt_epoch_comparison.png)

- `G-F2+DPO`: all 10 epochs pass the gates, articulation better than e14 at every epoch, event recall stays between 0.62 and 0.84. Epochs 2–10 form a plateau (composite 59–68). Epochs 6 and 10 were re-tested on unseen sentences and new seeds, and epoch 10 scored higher on the pooled data, so it is the released one. Epoch 2 scored highest on the first test set but fell back on unseen sentences.
- `G-F2` (no DPO): event recall drops to 0.47–0.53 from epoch 6 on, and on unseen sentences it failed the severe-error gate. `G-F` reached 0.53–0.72 event recall and was not re-tested on unseen sentences.
- `F` / `F2` (constant LR): large epoch-to-epoch swings.

SoVITS re-training did **not** beat the shipped epoch 4: pooled over two seeds (424 pairs) the best candidates scored 54.1 (95% interval 44.7–62.7) and 51.9 (44.6–61.6) against a baseline of 50, and paired with the new GPT the results went both ways (52.7 and 44.5). SoVITS was therefore left unchanged.

![Selection summary](assets/05_selection_forest.png)

### Limits of this evaluation

Two real references only; event recall on a small sentence set; the prosody metric barely separates systems; composite weights are a judgement call; automatic metrics cannot see the electronic artefacts described above. The released version was additionally accepted by listening to 30 random draws (10 stratified-random unseen sentences × 3 seeds) by the maintainer.

## Technical Specifications

- **GPT:** autoregressive transformer decoder over semantic tokens, 24 layers, hidden size 512, 16 heads, feed-forward 2048, semantic vocabulary 1025 (1024 + EOS), phoneme vocabulary 732, BERT features from `chinese-roberta-wwm-ext-large`, training clips up to 54 s.
- **SoVITS (v2ProPlus):** VITS-style generator that decodes semantic tokens conditioned on a reference clip and a speaker-verification embedding (ERes2NetV2 `sv/` model); 32 kHz output.
- **Software:** GPT-SoVITS `ea2d2a8`, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.4.0 (CUDA 12.4). **Hardware:** NVIDIA GPU recommended; see the CPU note above.

# WAXAL VoxCPM2 — Top-10 African TTS

A full fine-tune of [VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) (2B params, tokenizer-free, diffusion-AR TTS with voice cloning) on the **10 highest-resource languages** in the WAXAL/AfroNet collection, produced by the [WAXAL](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking) project at [LyngualLabs](https://lynguallabs.org).

This is a research checkpoint. It is not production-polished — see **Known Limitations** below before using it for anything beyond experimentation.

This model is trained on a **cleaned** version of the WAXAL/AfroNet pooled corpus (see **Data Cleaning** below), the same methodology used for its sibling models. It's the middle of three sibling models (Top-5 / Top-10 / all-28) trained from the same cleaned data, to compare whether language count or data quality matters more at this scale.

## Languages

VoxCPM2 has no built-in mechanism for specifying language at inference — the base model infers pronunciation purely from text orthography. We use a dedicated `<lang:XX>` tag per language, registered as a real token in the tokenizer and resized into the text embedding table (mean-initialized, then learned during fine-tuning). **The tag is mandatory** — always prepend it to the text you want synthesized, e.g.:

```
<lang:yo> Ẹ káàárọ̀! Báwo ni oorun rí lálẹ́ àná?
```

| Language | Tag | Hours after cleaning | Hours after resampling | Retention after cleaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Swahili | `<lang:sw>` | 922.8 | 689.9 | 96.4% |
| Kinyarwanda | `<lang:rw>` | 910.5 | 685.3 | 96.1% |
| Yoruba | `<lang:yo>` | 732.3 | 614.5 | 74.0% |
| Igbo | `<lang:ig>` | 620.2 | 565.6 | 69.6% |
| Hausa | `<lang:ha>` | 534.2 | 524.9 | 82.0% |
| Dholuo | `<lang:luo>` | 165.1 | 291.8 | 95.4% |
| Wolaytta | `<lang:wal>` | 141.1 | 269.7 | 78.1% |
| Amharic | `<lang:am>` | 154.5 | 282.3 | 86.6% |
| Oromo | `<lang:om>` | 151.1 | 279.1 | 85.7% |
| Sidama | `<lang:sid>` | 140.4 | 269.1 | 79.6% |

Source data: the [AfroNet](https://huggingface.co/Professor) speech collection (`Professor/<language>-speech-data`), after the Phase 1 cleaning pass described below. This checkpoint's base, `VoxCPM2_langtagged`, has exactly these 10 tags registered — no unused tag rows, unlike the Top-5 sibling model.

## Data Cleaning

Earlier releases in this collection (`voxcpm2-multilang28-full`, `voxcpm2-multilang10-full`, `voxcpm2-bantu8-full`) trained directly on the pooled raw corpus. This model and its Top-5 / all-28 siblings are trained on data that first passed through a dedicated cleaning pipeline, applied per language before any resampling:

1. **Clip/peak check** — reject clips with a sustained near-full-scale amplitude (likely clipped/distorted audio).
2. **Silence trim** — trim leading/trailing silence before any downstream check, so later checks evaluate the audio that's actually used for training.
3. **Duration-vs-text-length ratio check** — flag clips whose trimmed duration is a statistical outlier relative to their text length for that language. This caught a real upstream data bug: a small number of rows had their `text` field corrupted with concatenated Common Voice metadata (worst case, 225,940 characters for a single 9-second clip in the Luganda corpus).
4. **ASR-CER gate** — transcribe the trimmed audio with a small ASR model (`omniASR_CTC_1B`) and compare against the label text (CER threshold 0.3, diacritic/tone-mark-insensitive comparison so correct transcriptions aren't penalized for missing a tone mark the ASR doesn't produce).

Retention varies by language (69.6%–96.4% for this model's 10 languages — see table above). Yoruba and Igbo's lower retention is primarily genuine ASR-CER disagreement rather than bad data — both are tonal/diacritic-heavy languages where `omniASR_CTC_1B` performs less reliably.

## Training

- **Base**: `VoxCPM2_langtagged` — `openbmb/VoxCPM2` with 10 `<lang:XX>` tokens added and the text embedding table resized (mean-initialized rows) before any fine-tuning. Same tagged base reused for the Top-5 sibling model.
- **Mode**: full fine-tuning (all parameters trainable except the frozen AudioVAE codec).
- **Data balancing**: sqrt-temperature resampling (weight ∝ √hours, renormalized to preserve total volume) across the 10 languages, same methodology as the other models in this collection.
- **Scale**: 2,237,047 training rows (clips) after resampling, 4,297 held-out validation rows.
- **Steps**: 34,000 steps (~1.01 epochs over the resampled training set), batch size 3 × grad-accum 11 × 2 GPUs (effective batch 66).
- **Hardware**: 2× NVIDIA H200, via `torchrun` DDP.
- **Learning rate**: 1e-5, 100 warmup steps.
- **Final validation loss**: total 0.851 (diff 0.835, stop 0.016) at step 33,999.

## Usage

```python
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
from voxcpm import VoxCPM
import soundfile as sf

model_dir = snapshot_download("waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-top10-full")
model = VoxCPM.from_pretrained(model_dir, load_denoiser=False, optimize=False)

wav = model.generate(
    text="<lang:om> Akkam bultan?",
    cfg_value=2.0,
    inference_timesteps=22,
)
sf.write("out.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate)
```

`optimize=False` is required — `torch.compile` (the default optimization path) conflicts with some inference environments (e.g. HF ZeroGPU Spaces); disabling it costs some speed but avoids crashes.

Voice cloning works the same way as base VoxCPM2 — pass `prompt_wav_path` and `prompt_text` (the literal transcript of what's spoken in the reference clip) alongside the tagged `text`.

## Evaluation

**Pending.** The automated evaluation pipeline used for earlier releases (ASR-based CER against ground-truth text, a real-recording CER noise floor per language, and DNSMOS naturalness) has not yet been run against this checkpoint. Numbers from `voxcpm2-multilang28-full` are **not applicable here** — that model was trained on uncleaned data and is not a valid proxy for this model's quality. This section will be updated once Stage A/B/C evaluation has run.

## Known Limitations

- **No evaluation results yet** (see above) — training loss converging normally is not the same as verified downstream speech quality.
- **Yoruba and Igbo retained less data than most of the other languages** (74.0% and 69.6%) due to the ASR-CER gate disagreeing more often on these tonal/diacritic-heavy languages. We did not disable the CER gate for these two (unlike Somali/Ikposo in the all-28 cleaning pass, where drop rates were far more extreme at 70-80%) — their elevated-but-not-extreme drop rates were judged plausible rather than clearly an ASR-model artifact, but this is a judgment call, not a certainty.
- **Voice-design and cross-lingual flexibility are likely reduced**, consistent with what we've seen in other full-fine-tune checkpoints in this collection — full-FT on read-speech-only data tends to degrade the base model's text-prompted style/voice-design control and non-trained-language generation.
- **Non-terminating generation** was an observed failure mode in earlier releases on this same base model (see `voxcpm2-multilang28-full`'s model card); whether it recurs here is one of the things the pending evaluation will check.

## Related

- [`waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-top5-full`](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-top5-full) — the 5-language sibling model, same base checkpoint and methodology, a subset of this model's languages.
- [`waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang28-full`](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang28-full) and [`voxcpm2-multilang10-full`](https://huggingface.co/waxal-benchmarking/voxcpm2-multilang10-full) — earlier releases trained on the uncleaned pooled corpus.
- All-28 (clean-data) sibling model — trained the same way as this one, for comparison; linked here once released.
- [AfroNet speech collection](https://huggingface.co/Professor) — the source training data.

# Pocket TTS, Q8_0

[Kyutai's Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts) converted for Inklight, an iPhone app that reads books aloud on the device, and for PocketVoice Reader, a Firefox extension that reads web pages aloud. The FlowLM transformer reads all its weights once for every frame it generates, which makes it memory-bound on a phone; with its linear layers in Q8_0 it reads a quarter as much and renders about 30 % faster, and the file is little more than half the size of the original.

## Files

One `model.q8.gguf` per language, about 129 MB each: `english_2026-04`, `german`, `french`, `spanish` and `portuguese`, each the model of the same name from [kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning) (German, French, Spanish and Portuguese as of Kyutai's commit `1e08e6a` of 2026-10-01, the versions pocket-tts 4.0.1 uses), with the FlowLM transformer's linear weights in Q8_0 and every other tensor in F16. The Mimi encoder, which turns audio into latents and is only used to clone a voice, is left out; in the release without voice cloning its weights are not usable anyway. Tensor names are those of the original `model.safetensors`.

Each file needs the tokenizer and voice embeddings of its language from Kyutai's repository, which are unchanged and not copied here, and the slower voice states in [inklight-app/paced-voices](https://huggingface.co/inklight-app/paced-voices) load into the English one the same way.

## How it was made

With `quantize_model` in [goocy/pocket-tts-ios](https://github.com/goocy/pocket-tts-ios) (branch `aloud`), a fork of the Rust port [UnaMentis/pocket-tts-ios](https://github.com/UnaMentis/pocket-tts-ios), which also loads the file. It is the same conversion the app used to run on each phone after downloading the original. Against the full-precision model, the transformer's hidden state differs by about 2 % (4.5 % in the worst frame of a 25-second utterance), and in listening tests the differences between renders followed the random seed, not the precision.

## Credits and licence

This is an adaptation of [Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts) by Kyutai, licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) licence, and is released under the same licence. Kyutai's terms of use apply to it as to the original: it must not be used for voice impersonation or cloning without consent, to deceive, or to produce unlawful or harmful content.

Changes made: the transformer's linear weights were quantized to 8 bits, the other weights converted to 16-bit floats, and the voice-cloning encoder removed. Kyutai does not endorse these files or the apps. It is provided without warranty.

Lure Turbo 0.6B

The Lure voice, about 1.7x faster end to end. First audio in 135 to 170 ms on an H100.
Research preview · English · 0.6B parameters · 24 kHz · Lure · lure-tts engine

> [!WARNING] > **Research preview.** Weights, behaviour and this card can change between releases. Pin a revision if you build on it. ## What Turbo changes Lure, like every Qwen3-TTS 12Hz model, makes each 80 ms audio frame in two stages: a large model picks the first of the frame's 16 codes, then a small code predictor fills in the other 15, one after another. Those 15 sequential passes are most of the time spent per frame once the large model is fast. Lure Turbo replaces them with a head that predicts the 15 codes in **3 grouped passes** (codes 1-3, 4-7 and 8-15). Same 0.6B size, same voices, same tags and directions. | Per frame, L4, 8 streams | Lure | Lure Turbo | |---|---|---| | Code predictor passes | 15 | **3** | | Code predictor time | 21.2 ms | **6.2 ms** | ## Speed Measured with the [lure-tts](https://github.com/smirki/lure-tts) engine, cuda backend, bf16. RTF is generation time divided by audio length; TTFA is time to the first audio chunk. | GPU | Model | Streams | TTFA | RTF | |---|---|---|---|---| | H100 | Lure | 1 | 283 ms | 0.23 | | H100 | **Lure Turbo** | 1 | **168 ms** (135 ms with a 1-frame first chunk) | **0.14** | | H100 | Lure | 8 | 331 ms | 0.25 | | H100 | **Lure Turbo** | 8 | **200 ms** | **0.15** | | L4 | 1 stream | 8 streams, total | |---|---|---| | Lure | 2.3x real time | 17x real time | | **Lure Turbo** | **4.0x real time** | **30x real time** | ## Quality Turbo scores the same as Lure on every public benchmark we ran (one take per line, official scripts): | | Seed-TTS WER ↓ | Seed-TTS SIM ↑ | LibriSpeech-PC WER ↓ | LibriSpeech-PC SIM ↑ | UTMOS ↑ | VDB SIM ↑ | CV3 emotion % ↑ | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Lure | 1.51 | 0.653 | 1.72 | 0.638 | 4.43 | 0.81 | 73.3 | | Lure Turbo | 1.59 | 0.654 | 1.84 | 0.641 | 4.38 | 0.81 | 73.3 | The full comparison with other models is on the [Lure card](https://huggingface.co/smirki/lure-tts-0.6b-preview#benchmarks). ## Quick start The grouped head needs the [lure-tts](https://github.com/smirki/lure-tts) engine, which loads it automatically when `turbo.json` is in the model folder (mlx, cuda and C++ backends). Other Qwen3-TTS runtimes do not know the head. ```bash git clone https://github.com/smirki/lure-tts && cd lure-tts hf download smirki/lure-turbo-tts-0.6b-preview --local-dir models/lure-turbo pip install ./backends/mlx ".[server]" # Mac; see the repo for NVIDIA and the C++ build ``` ```python from lure_tts import Lure tts = Lure.load("models/lure-turbo") voice = tts.make_voice("reference.wav", "Transcript of the reference clip.", name="me") for pcm in tts.stream("(gasp) No way. (laugh) You actually did it!", voice, instruct="Bright, giddy disbelief."): ... # float32 chunks at 24 kHz ``` Tags, directions and recommended settings are the same as Lure's; see the [Lure card](https://huggingface.co/smirki/lure-tts-0.6b-preview#sound-tags). ## Limitations Same as Lure: English only, sound tags are best effort, and very long single calls should be split into sentences. # kairos-voice

Kyutai's **Pocket TTS** for the browser, French and English, mirrored so the [kaairos](https://kaairos.app) video
editor downloads files that cannot change under it. It reads a voiceover's words on the visitor's own machine, on
onnxruntime-web 1.30 (WebAssembly, one thread), and nothing is sent anywhere.

## Files

Two bundles in the `volume-board/pocket-tts-onnx@1` format, one per language: the flow language model's backbone
and flow head and the Mimi decoder (int8), the text embedding table (float16), the tokenizer, one predefined voice
(the flow model's attention cache after hearing the speaker, float16) and a manifest of shapes and generation
settings.

| folder | from | voice |
|---|---|---|
| `fr/` | [Vincweb/pocket-tts-french-onnx](https://huggingface.co/Vincweb/pocket-tts-french-onnx), byte for byte | Estelle |
| `en/` | exported from Kyutai's English weights with the same scripts (below) | Alba |

The sha256 of every file is in the kaairos repository, `training/voice/export.sha256`.

## What it is, and the terms

- **Pocket TTS** — Kyutai ([kyutai-labs/pocket-tts](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts), weights
  [kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts-without-voice-cloning)),
  **CC BY 4.0**. French weights at revision `1e08e6a23401048648a9fdcfde2f89348215c2a7`, English at
  `a7056f505a4a8ca72d8b5fb1440071d6f1a35739`.
- **Changes made**: a format conversion, not a new model — the PyTorch modules exported to ONNX with their streaming
  state as graph inputs and outputs, then dynamic int8 quantisation of the MatMul and Gemm weights
  (`onnxruntime.quantization.quantize_dynamic`). French converted by Vincweb; English by the kaairos project with
  Vincweb's scripts, pocket-tts 4.0.1, torch 2.14.1 (CPU). The English export was checked against PyTorch on one flow
  step (max difference 1.5e-6, end-of-speech logit −10.7658 both).
- **Voices**: Estelle — `kyutai/tts-voices`, `unmute-prod-website/developpeuse-3.wav`, CC0. Alba — Alba Mackenna,
  `kyutai/tts-voices`, `alba-mackenna/casual.wav`, CC BY 4.0.
- **Kyutai asks**, and so does this mirror: no voice impersonation or cloning without explicit and lawful consent, no
  deceptive use, and no presenting generated speech as a genuine recording of a real person or event.

# Breeze TTS 2 (BF16)

Derived from Breeze TTS 2 by BreezeBlue and licensed for research and non-commercial use only.

Native MLX checkpoint for [speech-swift](https://github.com/soniqo/speech-swift).
English and Chinese synthesis, natural-language voice design, reference-guided voice
cloning and direction, mono 24 kHz PCM, and incremental audio chunks.

Source: [BreezeBlue/Breeze-TTS-2](https://huggingface.co/BreezeBlue/Breeze-TTS-2/tree/3e28c5151381a722f1d8661b4118c298caa77aa4).
The model and self-hosted outputs are restricted to research and non-commercial use.
See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE). This is an independently converted checkpoint.

## Conversion

Unquantized BF16 Linear weights; embeddings, normalization weights,
and depth codebook heads retain upstream precision. The Qwen3 audio tokenizer is copied
unchanged. Unused legacy codec and text embeddings are removed; tied audio embeddings
are stored once. Immutable provenance, file hashes, and conversion details are in
`export_config.json`. No inference quality or performance claim follows from export alone.

## Swift

```swift
import BreezeTTS

let model = try await BreezeTTSModel.fromPretrained(modelId: "aufklarer/Breeze-TTS-2-MLX-bf16")
let samples = try await model.generate(
    text: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
    instruction: "A clear, calm English narrator.")
```

## CLI

```bash
speech speak "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog." --engine breeze \
  --breeze-model-id aufklarer/Breeze-TTS-2-MLX-bf16 --instruct "A clear English narrator" --stream -o speech.wav
```

Voice cloning requires `--voice-sample reference.wav --breeze-reference-text "Exact transcript"`.
Add `--instruct` to direct the reference voice. English and Chinese are inferred from text.
Use one generation at a time per model. Reaching the frame cap before EOS raises an error.

## Measured Swift smoke test — 2026-10-24

Apple M5 Pro, 48 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2, release build with compiled Metal
shaders. English voice design, 3.68 seconds of speech, seed 42, guidance 4,
3 frames in the first chunk and 25 thereafter. Three warm repeats.

| Metric | Measured |
|---|---:|
| Model load, cached local files | 1.391 s |
| First request, first decoded audio | 488 ms |
| Warm median, first decoded audio | 462 ms |
| Warm median RTF (wall/audio) | 1.258 |
| Peak RSS | 6.06 GiB |
| Peak physical footprint | 10.75 GiB |

RSS can undercount GPU mappings. Physical footprint includes MLX allocations
and reusable buffers. Other texts and reference modes can use more memory.
All measured clips for this checkpoint have zero normalized WER/CER with
`aufklarer/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-MLX-4bit`; see `validation.json` for transcripts,
per-request timing, memory, and numerical comparisons with official PyTorch.
All 16 measured clips across both published variants match the previous validated
WAV files byte for byte. The full local CI unit selection passed 1,739 tests
with 41 skips; all ten Breeze runtime/CLI E2E checks and three exporter checks passed.
This is a deterministic smoke test, not a general quality or speaker-identity benchmark.

Native Swift runtime, CLI, and regression coverage: [speech-swift #526](https://github.com/soniqo/speech-swift/pull/526).

## Audio samples

The unchanged Qwen3 audio tokenizer is separately licensed under Apache-2.0;
see [audio_tokenizer/LICENSE](audio_tokenizer/LICENSE) for its source attribution
and full license.
